en: Having prostrated before the Buddha, who is supreme in his cause for warding off the miserable paths and evil destinies,
I shall explain [this work], which is like a wish-fulfilling cow of virtue, according to the traditional transmission.
I shall proclaim the *Kalyāṇakāmadhenu*, marked by the solitary hero who has attained accomplishment (*siddhaikavīra*),
whose treasury is the coral of knowledge, and which has sprouted with the gems of phenomenal manifestation.

Regarding this, "to be manifested" means that through manifestation, that jewel is the *siddhi*. That itself is the *vaidūrya*, a particular kind of gem. The "treasury" (*kośa*) is the treasury that serves as its locus. Regarding the phrase "the mantra branch for accomplishing the solitary hero" (*ekavīrasādhana-mantrāṅga*): "solitary hero" refers to the mantra that is independent of [auxiliaries] such as mandalas and mudrās.

Because the qualities are gathered through the application of that mantra, it is a "limb" (*aṅga*), like a breast. "Sprouting forth" refers to the specific means for accomplishing the *siddhis*. It is a "jewel" (*ratna*) because it perfectly fulfills the desired aims. Its "shoot" (*aṅkura*) possesses horns (*śṛṅga*) resembling the shoots of a jewel; this refers to the treatise (*śāstra*). What is that very [treatise]? It is stated: "The Wish-Fulfilling Cow of Virtue" (*Kalyāṇakāmadhenu*).

This is the wisdom that follows after virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharma-anvaya-jñāna*). "Desire" (*chanda*) refers to the aspiration for them. Because it brings that desire to full completion, it is "nourishment" (*pusta*); it is like a cow of the treatise (*śāstra-dhenu*) endowed with the four limbs of the fourfold milk-yielding capacity.
And many prostrations to all mantras.
Having the nature of being produced from its own causes.
Therefore, even that which is indeterminate, |||
One should apply [the analysis] to the beginning and the end.

The phrase "all mantras" is connected with the expression "should be joined. Regarding "joined with *namas* and *svāhā*," this means they should be endowed with *oṃ* at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end. The phrase "even though not explicitly taught" means even when there is no direct instruction. By the words "beginning and end," and so forth, he indicates another point as well.

From the oral instructions of the guru who knows the reality of mantra, one understands the spreading of the mantra, the kindling of the mantra, the enhancement of the mantra’s brilliance, the satisfaction of the mantra, and the bringing of the mantra near. Regarding those, as for the spreading of the mantra: *oṃ sattva amukasya āyuḥ sarvān adhi rakṣa*—this is for protection.

For pacification, it is: *oṃ āmuka-sya śāntiṃ kuru svāhā*. For subjugation, it is: *oṃ sādhaya sādhaya rājyaṃ me kuru svāhā*. For the accomplishment of mantras, it is: *oṃ svāhā mantra-siddhiṃ me kuru svāhā*. For the removal of disease, it is: *oṃ namo namaḥ vyādhiṃ me apahara svāhā*. For enrichment, it is: [oṃ puṣṭiṃ me kuru svāhā].
For nourishment: *oṃ bhoṣa ta puṣṭiṃ me kuru svāhā*. For killing: *oṃ phaṭ amukaṃ hana hana hūṃ phaṭ*. For expelling: *hūṃ amukaṃ utsāraya hūṃ*. For summoning: *oṃ amukasya āmukagandhapāya svāhā*.

For great pacification, it is: *oṃ svāhā āmuka-sya āmukaṃ aupadravakṣaye svāhā*. For the ritual of driving in the kīla, it is: *oṃ kīli kīlaya sarvaṃ hūṃ*. One should understand these and others in this manner. For the rite of incineration (*sbar ba*), one should place a bindu upon the head of all mantras. For the rite of generating splendor (*gzi byin bskyed pa*), one should place the *nāda* [at the end].

For the purpose of satisfying, one should employ the syllable *khaṃ*; for the purpose of bringing near, one should employ the maṇḍala. These should be understood as the maṇḍalas of earth, water, fire, and wind, respectively.
Through familiarity with the inner-empty *gzi* stone, the precious essence is mastered.
One will undoubtedly attain high status.
Even by the power of the water of the grasping at dullness,
Whatever person it may be, they will become like that.

Regarding this: the word "inner" refers to the interior of the body. "Empty" means empty of self (*anātman*). "Splendor" (*tejas*) refers to splendor, which is the mandala of fire. "Wealth" (*vasu*) refers to Vasudhārā; "practiced" means trained through repeated cultivation. "Exalted" refers to the glory of exaltation (*abhyudaya*). "Transformation" (*vikāra*) means attainment.
In the same way, by practicing the water-mudrā of holding the neck, one will attain the heights of the high.

The application here is as follows: one should visualize a triangular mandala with the color of fire at the heart; upon that, an eight-petaled white lotus. On its petals, one should arrange the eight syllables of Vasudhārā: *oṃ vasudhāriṇi svāhā*. At the center, one should place the three syllables *bhrūṃ*, interspersing each syllable with the pair *yaṃ raṃ*.

In the cardinal directions, one should write the seed-syllables of the eight great yakṣas: Maṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Dhana-da, and Vaiśravaṇa in the four cardinal directions; and Kālimālinī, Piṅgakuṇḍalin, Mukhamaṇḍika, and Caturmukha in the intermediate directions—all of which end with *svāhā*.
The eight syllables of Jambhala, namely *oṃ jaṃ bhala jalandhrāya*, are to be placed upon an eight-petaled lotus; furthermore, the syllable *jaṃ* is to be placed in the central hub.

If one is unable to perform the meditative concentration, one should write two wheels correctly upon gold or other metal plates, join them together, place them inside butter and honey, and having performed worship, invite the wisdom wheel (*jñānacakra*) and dissolve it therein; then, one should offer worship every day with fragrant flowers and so forth.
Alternatively, if one places it in saffron water and makes offerings, one will attain the glory of the higher realms.
Regarding what is taught as "aoṃ tshinda," and whatever mantra there is called "hūṃ phaṭ," its syllables are arranged vertically as na-ma-na-ni.
Through familiarity with knowledge, blood and flesh will be summoned.

Regarding this, "mantra" refers to the mantra syllables: *oṃ chinda chinda vāsukasya raktam ānaya chinda chinda ākarṣaya hūṃ phaṭ*. "In the form of grains" means looking with eyes fixed like grains. "Su-su-ma" means the veins. "Knowledge" means knowing its application.

Abiding in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of whichever wrathful king (*krodharāja*) one pleases, one should visualize at the heart a red and blue *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* accompanied by blazing light. Having unified the two life-breaths (*prāṇa*), one draws them out from the right nostril like a thread; then, visualizing the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in front, those life-breaths become five-pointed and strike the object’s forehead, mouth, and heart.

Having pierced the vessels at the two head-joints, one should recite the mantra at intervals; then, by exhaling and drawing [the air] back in, one should cause blood to be drawn into the mouth or into a vessel. "Practice" (goms pa) means training through repeated cultivation.

[*Prathama] [incipit, 3 recto]: Taking some fruit in the hand, one should pierce it with the previously mentioned needle of the channels (*nāḍīsūcī*). Having stabilized it, one should then draw [the essence] in by means of the breath of exhalation until the juice of the fruit has entered the mouth. When it has been tasted, then, standing at a distance again, one should practice [this] even on objects such as a neem tree (*nimba*); the extraction of blood and so forth should be performed.
The heart-mantra of Mahiṣavāhinī is: *Nandini varade kiṇi 2*. Through one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*) and the offering of balls of *guggulu* resin, [the deity is propitiated].
It creates prosperity even for those who have committed misdeeds.

The mantra is: *oṃ nandini varade kiṇi 2 śriyaṃ me dada vauṣaṭ svāhā*. The procedure for this is as follows: Abiding in the *vajra-hūṃkāra* samādhi, one should emanate *Ṭakkirāja* from the heart; he is the supreme weapon, holding a hook and a noose in his hands. With him, one should draw forth Durgā—who rides upon a buffalo, has eight arms, and is dark green like emerald—and having established her before oneself, one should offer the *argha* water and recite this very mantra. When the recitation is finished, one should worship her once more and then dismiss her.

In this manner, one should recite until one hundred thousand [recitations] are completed during the three junctions of the day; thus is the preliminary service performed. Thereafter, one should offer oblations of guggulu resin pills, the size of cotton seeds and mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar, into a square fire-pit where a fire of *palāśa* wood is blazing, until one hundred thousand have been completed. Then, one attains great prosperity. || 4 ||
One should paint the southern [direction] as dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, and the western [direction] as variegated as a yakṣī.
As if her limbs were studded with stars by the shimmering of the clusters of gems from her ornaments.

"Dark-green like a blade of *dūrvā* grass" means she is green in color. She is one who should be depicted at night and not during the day, for by nature she is bashful like a trembling leaf. "Even" means she does not have uneven limbs; that is to say, she is gentle in appearance and endowed with the auspicious marks of all her limbs. Her limbs refer to the parts such as the face, ears, nose, eyes, eyelashes, teeth, and lips. She is "starred," meaning she is adorned by those very limbs.

By what kind of limbs? By those limbs whose radiance is like a cluster of blossoms from the jewels of their ornaments—that is, rays having the form of the spreading clusters of jewels belonging to whatever ornaments those limbs possess. That Yakṣiṇī, who is illuminated by those rays and is renowned by the name Vadhū, has this mantra:
"O Secret One, grant boons, O Secret One, you are perfected"—one should recite this one hundred thousand times.
Though repeated, that bride was no longer beautiful, for her luster had vanished like a fire whose sacred syllable (praṇava) has been lost.

Āḥ! O secret one, most excellent secret one, you are perfected; [protect] me, svāhā! Even if she is repeated or even if she is reviled, she is accomplished by this method. Regarding the phrase "the one whose praṇava is lost": in place of the syllable *oṃ*, there is the syllable *āḥ*. By this, she comes under control; the meaning is that she is accomplished. He explains how one accomplishes her:
Remaining silent, sleeping on the bare ground, bathing three times and changing clothes during the fortnight,
[he should worship] with eight hundred jasmine flowers.
Through what is desired, one obtains the desired boon.

He is silent, conversing only with his companion and with no one else who is not a fellow-practitioner. Having smeared an open space on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with cow dung, he should sleep upon a bed of *kuśa* grass. He bathes three times a day and changes his three garments; he also changes his white, pure clothes at the three junctions of the day.

Having invoked [the deity] as before and worshipped with fragrant flowers and other offerings, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the rule; thereafter, one should strike [the image] with eight hundred jasmine flowers while uttering the mantra for each individual blow: on the vulva for the sake of a wife, on the breast for the sake of a sister, on the foot for the sake of a mother, and on the head for the sake of a daughter-in-law.

[An addition in the upper margin in a crude second hand: Śvetāparājitā, 4 parts; Rudrajaṭā, 10 parts; Kṛtāñjali, 5 parts; Lajjālū, 9 parts. Having prepared an ointment with these and mixed with ghee...
[for those] whose crests are purified by images of Aṅguṣṭhamita, Sitārkī, and Gaṇapati, there shall be no defeat at dice for those who mutter the final syllable.

Having taken the root of the white *arka* plant with a flower, one should have an image of Gaṇapati made the size of a thumb; it should have four arms, a protruding belly, and a snake as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), with its hands holding a tusk, an axe, a noose, and a dice-cube. Holding that [image] in the hand—either through that specific yoga or through the yoga of one’s own tutelary deity—one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. Afterwards, having tied it upon the topknot, there shall be no defeat in gambling or games of chance; this is the meaning.
Of which men? Of those who recite the final syllable. "Final" means the end; it is the final syllable at the end of the fourth quarter of this very verse. This is its mantra: Oṃ gaḥ svāhā.
This *Mahāmayūrī-hṛdaya*, recited while encapsulated by the *praṇava* and *svāhā* of the immortal Jīvantī, accomplishes all rites.

The mantra is: *oṃ amaraṇijīvantīye svāhā*. This king of mantras, when well-recited, accomplishes all rites. By combining *nirguṇṭhī*, *picumarda*, and the down of a peacock feather together and offering incense with this mantra recited one hundred and eight times, all fevers will depart. Having consecrated oil for a headache, one should rub it on the head; headaches will be destroyed. By wiping away [the affliction], it destroys swellings, pustules, and the like.

In the case of an eruptive disease (sphoṭaka), one should give sandalwood water over which the mantra has been well-recited; it then pacifies the affliction. By means of the rite of fire-oblation (homakarman), one destroys all calamities caused by planetary spirits (graha) and the like. Having seized the hair of anyone whatsoever, the yogin—standing naked with disheveled hair, facing south, and seated upon the threshold of a house—should take that hair with both hands and recite the mantra. If he should crush it while enraged during the three junctions of the day (sandhyā), even a hero will die within three nights.
ARKĀRKIMARKĀRKI HRĪḤ NĀGAMAṆI PHAṬ— this is the Śābarikā mantra named Nāgamaṇi, which is perfected by reciting it one million times for the Kṛṣṇa-Śabaras.
With a peg made of khadira wood, fixed deeply in the region of the navel by means of piercing, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.

Oṃ namaḥ kṛṣṇaśabarāṇām arkārkimarkārki hrīḥ nāgamaṇi phaṭ. Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on fruits and roots, naked and in concealment, one should thereafter perform the ritual application (*prayoga*). Having fashioned an image of a woman made of *madana* wood, measuring one span (*vitasti*) and complete in all its limbs, one should inscribe the birth-name upon its forehead and the mantra upon its heart with *gorocanā* mixed with the blood from one’s own ring finger.

Having written [the mantra] on birch bark using the method of *vidarbhaṇa* and having inserted it [into the effigy], one should oneself assume the form of a *śabara*: with blood-red eyes, the mass of one's hair bound with peacock feathers, the ears adorned with the tips of ivory from young elephants, the lower part of the waist wrapped in the reddish tips of *aśoka* tree leaves, holding a goad and a noose in hand, and appearing as if devouring [the target] while standing facing the person to be subdued (*sādhya*). Having placed an image of the *sādhya* situated in the direction of the head of the [effigy]... [5 recto]... having made [it]... [5 recto]... having made [it]... [5 recto]... having made [it]... [5 recto]... having made [it]... [5 recto].

One should perform the ritual of staking with a stake made of *khadira* wood, the size of a thumb-joint, over which the mantra has been recited one hundred times. This is what is meant: one should bury a three-pointed spike made of *khadira* wood, smeared with lac-resin and consecrated by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, as if it were a nail driven into the private parts of the person to be acted upon. Afterwards, having provided red-colored offerings, one should repeat the mantra one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhya*). Within seven days, one will attract even Śacī, the wife of Indra; how much more so any other woman? "Krakrandura" refers to the female organ (*bhaga*). (8)
The mantra *cchavirali hūṃ phaṭ*, when recited and placed within the mouth upon a birch leaf,
draws [beings] from the sky.
His lap was marked with the sign of rabbit's blood.

The mantra is: *oṃ cchavirali hūṃ phaṭ*. This is its application: First, one should visualize a wind-maṇḍala in the sky before oneself by means of the syllable *yaṃ*; upon that, one should mentally conceive the person to be subdued (*sādhya*)—dark red in color—with his heart pierced by a goad made of excrement and his throat bound with a noose. When the visualization has become very clear, one should subsequently recite the mantra in secret. By reciting it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣajāpa*), one effects an attraction. How so?

Having drawn an image of the person to be accomplished on birch bark with rabbit blood, complete with all its limbs, and having inscribed the birth-name on the forehead, one should wrap it, place it inside a *madanaguli* pill, put it in one's mouth, and recite the mantra; thus, one causes [the person] to be drawn forth. (If one recites it, one draws that person forth.)

There is another application for this very [rite]: having drawn the two forms of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*) on a birch-bark leaf with the blood of a hare; having written the name of the person to be acted upon on the forehead of the practitioner’s form and the other name on the forehead of the person to be acted upon; and having joined these two together so that they meet face-to-face, forehead-to-forehead, and private part-to-private part, one should place them in one's lap so that they are heated by the heat from one's chest. One should recite the mantra in secret. Within three nights, one brings [the person] under control. 9.
"Stay! Bind! Hold! Restrain! Repeat from the beginning;
'ūrṇāmaṇi' is the last [word]."
This is the supreme [method] for the rite of binding the throat with the *ūrṇā*.

The application for this is as follows: *Oṃ he he tiṣṭha 2 bandha 2 dhāraya 2 nirundha 2 ūrṇāmaṇi svāhā*. Having consecrated ashes with this mantra, one should perform a binding of the throat with the index finger using forceful application; it wards off the vomiting of anyone whatsoever. Having written the mantra interspersed with the name of the enemy on a palm leaf (*tālapatra*), one should place it in a hole in a crab; it effects a binding of the mouth. Likewise, it paralyzes (*stambhayati*) another’s village or similar property even while it is being given away. At the end, [the word] *dantili* is in the middle.
"Mohani mucili" was previously indicated;
this mantra, with "svāhā" inserted throughout, is the Svapnamāṇavaka.

The procedure for this is as follows: *Oṃ mucili svāhā | mohani svāhā | dantili svāhā*. This is the mantra. Having fashioned a small mandala out of cow dung that has not fallen to the ground before the Guru, the Noble Avalokiteśvara, and having performed worship with flowers and other offerings, one should consecrate one's face with this mantra seven times. One should then sleep right there upon a clean cloth spread out; whatever purpose one has contemplated, one will see it exactly as desired, occurring in a dream.
Likewise, through drinking water or oil, or from anointing the face, one sees [these things] as they truly are in a dream. 11.
Oṃ [excise] cunde cute cale; thus, from the row of words being grasped in reverse order,
she who stands in the mirror speaks.
The objects characterized by the three times.

The application for this is as follows: *Oṃ cale cule cunde darśaya 2 sarvaṃ svāhā*. One should perform ten thousand recitations of this according to the ritual of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*). Thereafter, having honored a boy or girl who is not yet defiled by sexual intercourse, who is well-bathed, dressed in clean garments, adorned with ornaments, and protected by the mudrā and mantra of Noble Acala—namely, the mantra: *Oṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ*.

One should release two *tāla* measures for the *vajrabandha*, two *tāla* measures for the pair of suns (*ravi*), and another two *tāla* measures; this is the mudrā of Noble Acala. Having performed the binding of the directions, boundaries, and the sky with this very [mudrā] together with the mantra-mudrā, one should place a flask in the center of the maṇḍala, filled with scented water, its neck bound with a fresh white cloth, adorned with a garland, and its mouth decorated with sprouts. Then, having performed worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, [one should gaze] at the eyes of a boy and a girl facing the east.

Having placed two *oṃ* syllables on the two eyes and having visualized a radiant *cuṃ* syllable situated between two *oṃ* syllables in the heart, one should contemplate the Blessed Lady in the sky, born from the syllable *cuṃ*, seated upon a lunar disc, possessing the luster of the moon, holding an alms-bowl in her two hands and a lotus and a sword in the other two; then, having offered the *argha* and so forth to her, worshipped and praised her, [one should perform the rite] with one's own root-mudrā and mantra.

One should cause [the mantra] to enter the hearts of the boy and the girl: *oṃ cale cule cunde praviśa praviśātra kumārakumārikayoḥ śarīre praviśya darśaya sarvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ yathāsatyaṃ buddhadharmasaṅghasatyena bhagavati mā vilamba mama āśāṃ prapūraya svāhā*.

Then, one should show a mirror, a sword, a very clean thumb, a lamp, or a vessel of water over which the mantra has been recited to the boy or girl. As he gazes at it truthfully, one should dismiss him and he should rise.
The six syllables "varada svāhā" together with the *praṇava* (oṃ) propitiate Gaṇapati;
[he] is situated within a square maṇḍala.
The image [is attained] through worship for six months.

The mantra is: *Oṃ varada gaḥ svāhā*. Having prepared a square mandala with cow dung, one should, in a secluded place and alone, install an image or a cloth painting of Gaṇapati upon that mandala. Having worshipped him in the form of Vināyaka, one should perform the recitation (*jāpa*). By reciting this mantra one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day for six months, it fulfills one's heart's desire. It should be practiced while remaining naked.
O you with whirling hair, O you who cause whirling, whirl! O delusion, bewilder, infatuate! Svāhā!
This is the first mantra, repeated twice.
Furthermore, this [word] is non-denotative of a bee.

The mantra is: *oṃ bhrama bhramakeśi bhramamāte bhrama vibhrama muhya mohaya ūrṇe svāhā*. The first word, *bhrama*, should be pronounced twice. The line beginning with *ali* is to be recited exactly as it stands. That line which is accompanied by *ūrṇā* is called *sorṇā*. Even when unaccomplished, this [mantra] performs all rites.

Having placed a handful of mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*) in the air over the food, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*). Afterwards, taking a few mustard seeds from there, one with disheveled hair and loosened waistband should scatter them at the threshold of the house. By the mere act of stepping upon the mustard seeds, everyone is overcome by an untimely sleep until sunrise; this is the ritual procedure for inducing sound sleep (*susvāpana*).
Kiṇi 2 Ghaṇṭākarṇa, show me a dream, svāhā!
[This is accomplished] by drinking water over which this has been consecrated.
It reveals the truth within dreams.

[Emendation: However, by means of the yoga of one’s own deity, or through the *vajrahūṃkāra-samādhi*, [one should visualize] the one with the *karṇagaṇa* [ornament], whose two hands ring with bells, who is white in color, four-armed, and holds a trident, an axe, a noose, and a skull-cup in his hands; having seen him, one should bind the *samayamudrā* and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. Worship should be performed. With the left hand, one should display the trident, which is the *samayamudrā*.
Then, by drinking water consecrated with mantras, he speaks the truth in a dream. Of this there is no doubt. 15.
One should offer ten million *jātī* flowers into the waters of the ocean’s current with the mantra:
*oṃ vākyedaṃ namaḥ*.
The heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī, the Bestower of Boons.

Having descended into a river flowing toward the ocean, one should stand in water reaching up to the neck (or, according to another reading, the waist) and cast each bud of a *jātī* flower into the current while reciting the mantra. Among those buds thus cast forth, one will come back against the current; that one should be quickly swallowed with the water, without being touched by the teeth. This bestows the power of retaining what has been heard (*śrutidhāritā*).
Oṃ kurukulle svāhā;
this heart-mantra of Tārā is renowned for the rite of subjugating the three worlds.
This has been explained in the procedure for binding the jewel-necklace.

Having previously performed service to Tārā through the Halāhala-samādhi, one should thereafter, on an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, perform worship and draw a sixteen-spoked wheel in the shape of a blue lotus petal upon birch bark. Having assigned the sixteen digits (*kalā*) to the sixteen spokes, one should place the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the hub, constrained by the four syllables "Kurukulle," and encircled on the outside by the syllable *Oṃ* tripled. In the same manner, one should draw a second wheel, but without the name of the person to be accomplished.

Having stabilized this previous wheel, having as if directly invoked the Blessed Lady and worshipped her, and having caused the one to be subdued (*sādhya*) to enter that wheel, he sees him fallen at the feet of the Blessed Lady like a tree whose roots have been severed, being drawn in by the rays of all the syllables. Reciting the mantra three thousand times at the three junctions of the day for seven days, he brings even Śakra under his control.

Oṃ kurukulle phaḥ, bring such-and-such a person, together with his wealth and retinue, under my control, phaḥ svāhā! After seven days have passed, the wheel should be placed in the midst of curd, honey, and ghee.
By reciting the mantra three million six hundred thousand times, one obtains a woman whose pleasure is unknown [to others],
through the offering of white *darani* flowers.
Or else, [the offering] of those who have borne fruit.

A maiden who has not experienced the pleasure of sexual union—one such as this he obtains. How? That which consists of six, three, and the first (ādi), namely the beginning, is "six-three-first" (*ṣaṭtryādi*). Therefore, according to the ritual of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should perform recitation (*japa*) while abstaining from food containing liquor, meat, and the like, wearing wet clothes after bathing, and remaining silent. [The mantra is: *oṃ adite, give me such-and-such a maiden; cause her to be given, svāhā*. When a hundred thousand [recitations] are completed:

A hundred thousand oblations (*lakṣahoma*) should be performed with each individual syllable, or one hundred thousand with white *arka* flowers or *priyaṅgu* blossoms. Having written the maiden’s name enclosed within one’s own name on birch bark or similar material, one should place it upon one’s lap and offer the oblations. In every respect, that maiden shall not be given to anyone other than him. 18.
Oṃ dicce mohe svāhā; recited seven times together with the *praṇava*,
this is the heart-mantra of Raṇḍāyakṣī.
Seven hundred thousand recitations are to be performed.
On a cloth depicting the concealment of the deceased,
her form as a widow— unadorned and marked with red lac— is to be worshipped.
Then, having worshipped the deity of manifold forms with yellow flowers, success is attained.
O you who possess flowers as your ornaments, all the widows existing within the three worlds stand at your service.
A female corpse prepared by means of consuming [her] for a month [is subdued] by the recitation of the heart-mantra.

The mantra for this is: *oṃ vicce mohe svāhā*. One should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) by reciting it seven hundred thousand times. Afterwards, having taken a piece of cloth from the shroud of a deceased Brahmin widow, one should draw that very form of the widow—without ornaments—on a square piece of cloth measuring one cubit, using the lac-dye from her own [feet]. Then, having established the cloth in a secluded place and performed worship with yellow *sāla* flowers alone, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) eight hundred times at night in the darkness.

She arrives after six months; once arrived, she should be desired. Having cast a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [gold pieces] upon the bed, she departs day by day. She must not be spoken to. When the full six months have passed, with the completion of those six months, she accomplishes all goals. 19.
Oṃ gaurī rudradayite yogeśvari [mukhavi? hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is released from the mouth of Gaurī (or, applied to the mouth).
The heart of the daughter of the mountain king.
One should write the name on the left thigh,
covering it with the left hand; while reciting the mantra, this attracts a woman (and, for metrical reasons, it also attracts food).
Immediately [he sees] a man on the right side.

Oṃ gauri rudradayite yogeśvari hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! During a lunar eclipse, having performed the worship of Gaurī with golden ochre, cow bezoar, or realgar, one should place these on seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, cover them with another seven [leaves], and placing the left hand upon them, recite the mantra as long as the moon is eclipsed. Having written the name of a woman in the middle of her left thigh with that [substance], and pressing it with the left hand, one should recite until she arrives.

If she is not bound, then for the purpose of bringing a man, one should likewise inscribe her name between the thighs of the right leg; having stepped upon it with the right hand, one should recite the mantra. In this way, his arrival occurs. This is the "drawing by the foot" (pādākṛṣṭi). 20.
The mantra is *praṇava*,
followed by *vidārīkuru* (emended from *vaidārīkuru*), *hūṃ phaṭ*; this is the *āptalipi* for the rite of subjugating the planets.
It has been recited, sealed, and dispatched.

The mantra is: Oṃ vaidārīkuru (emended from *vidārikuru*) hūṃ phaṭ. This mantra of Noble Acala, by means of the Vajra-krodha-samādhi, should be written according to the conventions of calligraphy, rolled up in a leaf, and sealed; it should then be dispatched into the hand of one seized by a planetary spirit (*graha*), where it should be placed so that Rudra releases [the victim].
21. Having spoken "Oṃ bhadravati vidāri svāhā," this ten-syllable vidyā is declared.
One brings the queen of the king under one's control;
this is not false, for it is accomplished by merely reciting [the mantra]. 22.
Oṃ (excise) mālini kiṇi 2; this mantra,
preceded by the sun [oṃ] and joined at the end with svāhā,
belongs to Sarasvatī for the sake of people.
He creates the speech of Sarasvatī.

The mantra is: *oṃ arkamālini kiṇi 2 svāhā*. Having first performed a preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) of one hundred thousand recitations of this mantra before Sarasvatī, one should thereafter take a handful of clarified butter from Sarasvatī, recite the mantra over it seven times, and drink it. Within a month, it bestows the eloquence of Sarasvatī. Likewise, by drinking water [with the same procedure], it does so within a month. By drinking clarified butter alone for six months, it bestows divine speech. 2.
O you with shaven heads, O you who are Piśācinīs by hearing! O you who are Piśācinīs by hearing!
This mantra, accompanied by a lamp, is for those who listen in secret.
He describes it in the left ear as that very same sequence of words in reverse order.

[Emendation: *paṅktiḥ*! Oṃ śravaṇapiśācini muṇḍe svāhā! By means of this [mantra], one who sleeps on a bed with *kuṣṭha* [powder] applied to both feet and the face perceives a dream—whether auspicious or inauspicious; there is no doubt. 2.
Having gathered it for one fortnight...
Oil-cake is prescribed for the Mountain Maiden;
by offering oblations of bilva fruits smeared with clarified butter,
one shall obtain a kingdom— of this there is no doubt.
Mantra: Oṃ girikumārike māte rājyaṃ me sādhaya 25.
For a girl afflicted by *gi*, *kumārikā*,
*durga*, or *vidurginī*,
[there is success] from a hundred oblations with fuel-sticks of milky trees (*kṣīradruma*).
At night, independent of preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), he certainly bestows a village upon men.

The mantra is: *oṃ durge vidurgeṇi svāhā*. At the conclusion of the oblation—performed with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *vaṭa* and *aśvattha* trees and the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same age—while pronouncing the name of the village, one obtains the village. 33. (!?)
"Obeisance to Megholkā, svāhā"— this is the heart-mantra of Kiraṇamālin, accompanied by the praṇava;
one should give a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
But by means of a hundred thousand oblations of palāśa fuel-sticks.
The mantra is: *Oṃ megholkāya svāhā*. For Gaṇapati: *Oṃ khagolkāya svāhā*. For Kiraṇamālin: both of these yield the same fruit.
*Karṇāmoṭī*, accompanied by *hūṃ phaṭ* and recited four hundred thousand times.
By offering mustard seeds in the fire for a single day, one may attract even the three worlds.

The mantra is: *oṃ karṇāmoṭī amukam ākarṣaya hūṃ phaṭ*. This mantra, when recited four hundred thousand times before Cāmuṇḍā, subsequently draws a woman or a man within a single day by means of an oblation of *rājikā* seeds in a fire of *khadira* wood. 28.
Collyrium produced from the heartwood of a red lotus, consecrated with mantras over red substances,
brings good fortune even in the theater of hell.
It was thoroughly saturated with those sprinklings of fat.
The mantra is: *oṃ rakte raktini svāhā*. She is to be accomplished through all red-colored offerings.
O Candramukhī Kālī, this [mantra] has been recited through the contemplation of the lamp at the beginning and the end.
This one with the *ūrṇā* brings the entire circle of the earth under the state of obedience. Oṃ candramukhi kāli ūrṇe svāhā. 30.
With the mantra "Svāhā to Kandarpa," one who has been burnt by collyrium [is restored] through the application of collyrium; thus,
he makes even the offspring of the best of elephants fortunate.
Mixed with *tamāla* leaves and blue lotuses.

The mantra is: *Oṃ kandarpāya svāhā*. [One should take] elephant-ichor produced from the body of a noble elephant, *tamāla* (the leaf of the *tamāla* tree), and the petal of a blue lotus. Wearing red garlands and garments, with one's body anointed with red sandalwood, and having performed the protective rites with the well-recited mantra, [one should apply these as collyrium]. Note: *anupāttam* refers to that which has not yet been employed for the purpose of applying collyrium.

On either of the two dark lunar days, having performed the protective rites and so forth at the mother’s shrine, at a crossroads, or in a cremation ground, one should grind blue collyrium into powder, place it in a copper vessel, insert it into the vagina of a woman whose husband has passed away, seal it tightly, and burn it.

When it has been burnt, one should take it, bring it home, draw a mandala of Kāmadeva, and perform worship. Having mixed it with *tamāla* leaves, blue lotuses, and elephant ichor, and having placed it in a silver or golden vessel, one should set it within the mandala and consecrate it one hundred and eight or one thousand times. One whose eyes are anointed with this becomes like Kāmadeva to women. Having cast it into a man’s heart and burnt it, it is a means for subjugating men. 31.
The perfected one who delights the eyes and mind,
[who is] ablaze with the ten-fold matted locks born of fragrance.
Collyrium produced from the ghee of tawny cows and the *jaṭikā* plant is an incomparable means for making one beloved.
The mantra is: Oṃ nayanamanohari svāhā. The remainder is easy to understand. 32.
"Oṃ kāmasare svāhā"— this *kāmasara* mantra, when recited over collyrium that has been scorched by the mouth of a snake, brings others under one's control.
Karṇikā, nakha, tagara, and kuṣṭha, ground together with bhramara and aguru.

*Kamasa rasvāhā*. If one burns snake-skin and eye-medicine, along with *ruta*, Chinese incense (*jātī*), *ākārṇaka*, and elephant-hide, and binds it with lion-skin, one will bring others under one's power.

The mantra is: *oṃ kāmasare svāhā*. Having previously performed ten thousand recitations (*ayutapūrvasevā*), one should take elephant claw together with blue collyrium (*nīlāñjana*) that has been burnt according to the ritual for Kandarpa. Then, having combined it with *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, bees, and *aguru*, one should grind it into a fine powder, seal it as before, and recite the mantra eight thousand times. This is the collyrium (*añjana*) that brings the entire world under control. "Bees and *aguru*" refers to black *aguru* (*kṛṣṇāguru*). 33.
Oṃ ṣṭroṃ bandha— this collyrium is to be known as the soot that brings those who are not under control under one's power; [it is produced] from the abundant sprinkling of *kaṅgu* seeds.
Collected from the places where the horses' hooves had stood.

The mantra is: *oṃ ṣṭroṃ bandha svāhā*. Having fashioned a small vessel from a horse’s hoof and filled it with a sprinkling of *kaṅgu* grain, one should collect soot (*kajjala*) in that horse-hoof vessel using another horse-hoof vessel. Having performed worship before the Blessed One, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, one should consecrate [the substance]. [The ingredients are] a sprinkling of *kaṅgu* grain and *jyotiṣmatī* oil. *Oṃ*, this excellent mantra, joined with the first and last syllables...
He remains present for those who recite [his mantra] incessantly,
[rendering] the three worlds in a state of servitude.

Oṃ, O best of mantras, bring such-and-such a person, together with myself, along with their wealth and retinue, under my control, svāhā! Having visualized in one's mind the one whom one wishes to bring under control, one should perform the recitation; that person will follow as a servant. 35.
Fashioned upon a human head with the cord of a twice-born man by the friction of the feet of Caṇḍeśvara, it causes fever within a few days. (And in the case of food, Caṇḍeśvara...)
And the fierce one named Arāti is Dhuna.

Oṃ dhuna caṇḍa, kill [the person named] so-and-so with fever! Hūṃ phaṭ! [This is to be performed] upon a human head in a human skull. "Dvija" means a Brāhmaṇa; having made a rope from his hair, [one should act]. Caṇḍeśvara is Mahādeva. His "removed *nirmālya*" refers to the floral offerings removed from him (i.e., the food remains removed from him). "Caraṇa" means the dust from the feet of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Having combined everything and placed it in a skull-cup, one should recite the mantra repeatedly while churning with a human shank-bone and pulling [the mixture] with a rope made from the hair of a twice-born; by doing so, even a great person is afflicted with fever within three nights. 36.
The seven-syllabled Yakṣī, joined with the beginning and the end, should be fully understood:
*bhaga-bhugā* bestows good fortune upon the vulva.
Having recited it four hundred thousand times.

The mantra is: Oṃ bhage bhuge svāhā. Indeed, when this mantra has been recited four hundred thousand times while subsisting on a diet of black gram (māṣa), the widows residing in the three worlds will become submissive.
That is to say, having recited the sixfold [mantra] thirty-seven times while holding water in the hollow of the palms,
one beholds the yakṣa and yakṣī face to face.
By means of oblations of fuel-sticks from the banyan tree at the northern edge of the village, smeared with the three sweets.

At dawn, one should offer six handfuls of water into the midst of the water above the solar disc. Beneath a banyan tree to the north of a village, for one who performs a fire sacrifice with banyan wood-fuel smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), he beholds a yakṣa or a yakṣī face-to-face. The mantra is that same one previously mentioned: *oṃ bhage bhuge svāhā*. Once it has been mastered, she grants whatever boon is desired to whomever it pleases. 38.
In a forest lake or on a preeminent mountain, she remained for a fortnight,
subsisting on a diet of vegetables and offerings.
It bestows heroic victory and the status of a supreme universal monarch in the sky.

OḤ KHAṂ VĪRA! For one who dwells for one fortnight with offerings accompanied by wrath, this king of mantras, which brings victory, bestows the sovereignty of a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas* among those proceeding to the realm of the gods. 39.
"Oṃ rudriṇi svāhā"— this six-syllable heart-mantra of Umā, when recited,
fulfills one's desires.
Of those who have given birth to new fruit.
Phalinī is priyaṅgu; its flower-homas bring about great nourishment. 40.
The *Hṛdaya* of Gaṇapati, the Conqueror of Hosts,
accompanied by the *praṇava*, joined with the word "namas," and endowed with the "lamp" (*dīpaka*), when recited one hundred thousand times;
The practitioner should always perform [this] before the fire-oblation.

It brings victory everywhere in the midst of the assembly. What is this "Victory over the Assembly"? It is the Heart of Gaṇapati; how does it effect victory? By offering incense (*guggulu*) before it as an oblation: *oṃ gaṇa namaḥ gaṇajaya svāhā* (41).
The *Kalyāṇakāmadhenuvivaraṇa* is completed.
